classical

Cic. Fam. 9.24.3: cūrā ut valeās; id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre
Cic. Sen. 21: crēdō, nisi eam exerceās
Traupman 334

id (is, ea, id)

pronoun: neuter of is; genitive ejus, dative eī

it (of a thing; of a fact or an idea)

The neuter is for what has no gender in Latin: a fact, a clause, a deed (id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre). A noun keeps its own gender, so “it” is eam for memoria and eum for hortus. Very often Latin says nothing for “it”: as subject the verb carries it, and an object that is plain from the context is left out (Plaut. Aul. 641, ostendī, I’ve shown them).

Other words

  • verbum impersōnāle — it (in “it is raining”, “it is getting dark”)

    construction: the verb alone in the third person singular · classical · Ter. And. 581: jam advesperāscit; Quint. 6.3.66: nōn pluit, nōn opus est tibi

    Weather, time and feeling verbs have no subject at all: pluit, it is raining; advesperāscit, it is getting dark; mē paenitet, I am sorry. Never id pluit.

  • 1hic: short i (Lewis & Short hīc, haec, hōc, marking the heavy syllable as a long vowel). De Vaan 284, s.v. hic: the nominative is *hi-ke, so the vowel is short and the syllable heavy (hicc, p. 102, s.v. -ce); the adverb hīc, here, is the old locative *hoi-ke. Likewise the neuter hoc (hocc), against the ablative hōc.

    hoc1 — it, this (here, just said)

    pronoun: neuter of hic · also used · classical · Plin. Ep. 1.11.1: at hoc ipsum scrībe

    Pointing at the thing present or the point just made: Quid est hoc? What is it?

Examples

  • nōn pluit, nōn opus est tibi; sī pluit, ipse ūtar

    If it isn’t raining, you don’t need it; if it is raining, I’ll wear it myself.Quint. 6.3.66

  • jam advesperāscit

    It’s getting dark already.Ter. And. 581

  • Dīc mihi, aufūgistīne? — Era, factum. — Satin' id tibi placet? — Nōn. … Ūnam hanc noxiam mitte: sī aliam admīserō umquam, occīditō.

    Tell me, did you run away? — Yes, madam. — Are you pleased with it? — No. … Let me off this one fault: if I ever do another, kill me.Ter. Eun. 850–853

  • at memoria minuitur. crēdō, nisi eam exerceās

    But memory fades. — I suppose it does, if you don’t exercise it.Cic. Sen. 21

  • corium dēpressum in fluviō vīdērunt canēs. id ut comēsse extractum possent facilius, aquam coepēre ēbibere: sed ruptī prius periēre quam quod petierant contingerent

    Some dogs saw a hide sunk in a river. To get it out and eat it more easily, they began to drink up the water; but they burst and died before they reached what they were after.Phaedr. 1.20.3–6

  • cūrā ut valeās; id forīs cēnitandō facillimē cōnsequēre

    Look after your health; you’ll manage it most easily by dining out a lot.Cic. Fam. 9.24.3

See also he, she, its, it’s getting dark, it looks like rain.
